t: all who are disqualified for the service are permitted to slaughter sacrifices in the first instance. See also Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 9:6.

and even though he is outside the Temple courtyard and stretched out his hand and slaughtered inside the courtyard. For by Torah law it is permitted for a ritually impure person to put his hands into the courtyard (see ibid. 3:18).
even though it was said of it, "and Aaron shall slaughter". And in the first instance its slaughter is by the High Priest (Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 1:2).
even a red heifer slaughtered by a non-priest is valid. And in the first instance its slaughter is by a priest (see Hilchot Parah 4:3).
like one who is engaged in something else. He was handling the knife and slaughtered without intending to slaughter.
these are invalid. In contrast to the slaughter of unconsecrated animals, which does not require the intention to slaughter (Hilchot Shechitah 2:11).
and one shall not slaughter two heads as one among sacrifices. And with unconsecrated animals one slaughters this way in the first instance (Hilchot Shechitah 2:9 and Babylonian Talmud, Chullin 29a).
two who slaughter one animal. They hold the knife together.
like unconsecrated animals. Hilchot Shechitah 2:10.
even though the adult stands over him. And with unconsecrated animals, slaughter in front of an adult who watches the slaughter is valid (Hilchot Shechitah 4:5).
it is not a thought to be lenient. To make the sacrifice valid.
but to be strict. See Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 14:2.

if a burnt offering was standing in the south and he drew it etc.. The slaughter of a burnt offering is valid only on the north side of the altar, and since he draws it there, it is evident that he slaughters it as a burnt offering.
most holy offerings. Their slaughter and the receiving of their blood are in the north of the altar (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 5:2).

and he stretched his hand to the north and slaughtered, his slaughter is valid... and he stretched out his hand and received the blood in the north, his receiving is invalid. For in slaughter we follow the location of the animal, and in receiving the blood we follow the location of the priest receiving it.
he slaughtered it in the north and it convulsed and went out to the south... valid. Its slaughter is valid.

it convulsed and went out to the south and returned to the north and afterward he received its blood in the north, valid. Since the slaughter and the receiving were in the north, even though in the middle the animal went out to the south.
offerings of lesser holiness. Their slaughter and the receiving of their blood may be anywhere in the courtyard (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 5:2).
and its forelock. The hair of its head.

the animal convulsed and went outside after the receiving of its blood, valid. But if it left the courtyard before the receiving of the blood, the blood is disqualified (Har HaMoriah, Aruch HaShulchan 123:21).
as will be explained. Below, halakhot 32-33.
and afterward it put its foot outside etc.. And the flesh of most holy offerings that left the courtyard is disqualified and there is no remedy in returning it.
he cuts the flesh until he reaches the bone. And he does not cut the bone itself, so as not to make the animal lacking (see below, halakhah 29).

because of the fattiness of the flesh outside. The fat of the flesh of the leg, which was disqualified as a result of going outside the courtyard, mixes with the blood that is received in the receiving of the blood and disqualifies it.
for the flesh of offerings of lesser holiness that left before the sprinkling is valid. Accordingly the fattiness in the flesh that is absorbed into the blood is valid (Na'am David).
on the thigh of the altar. The slaughter should be in the place adjacent to the altar.
the signs. The windpipe and the gullet; one must slaughter at least most of the windpipe and most of the gullet (Hilchot Shechitah 1:9).
for slaughter exists from the beginning until the end. Slaughter is a continuous act from its beginning to its end, and every stage in it is part of this sequence (see also ibid. 4:13).
for this is not the manner of service. It was not done in the way in which it is proper to serve in the Temple.
the basin. The vessel in which the blood is received.
and received the blood in the air. When the basin is not resting on the ground.
for the air of a place is like the place. And it has the law of the courtyard itself.
a kind with its own kind is not a separation. The outer basin does not separate between his hand and the inner basin in which the blood is received (for this principle, see Hilchot Shofar 1:5).
he placed fibers inside the basin. Palm fibers tangled densely together (similar to a sponge; see the illustration on the previous page).
and took a handful from the fibers. And the fine flour was lying on the fibers in the vessel.
invalid. For the taking of a handful must be done from within a vessel, and the fine flour is not considered as placed in the vessel.
and likewise carrying limbs to the ramp. Bringing the limbs of the offerings that are to be burned to the ramp, in order to take them up to the altar and burn them.
as we have explained regarding taking the handful of the meal offering. Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 12:23.
and in pinching the bird's neck. This law was not mentioned explicitly until here (see Har HaMoriah, who cited there 6:20, and see below, 7:1).
and carrying not by foot is not carrying. Extending the blood and throwing it to the altar without moving the feet.
and he stood in his place and threw it to the altar, the sacrifice is disqualified. For the blood was thrown without carrying, and carrying is one of the services required in a sacrifice.

he received in his right hand and put it into his left, he should return it to his right. Since the receiving was done properly, the sacrifice was not disqualified when he transferred it to the left hand. But if he received in the left, it is invalid, for all services must be with the right hand (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 5:18).
it spilled from the vessel onto the floor and he gathered it, valid. For the blood was initially received properly in the vessel.
and he received some of it from the animal's neck. He received in a vessel the remaining blood in the neck.
that this blood that was received be the blood of the life. The blood by which the life departs, which is the blood fit for the altar.
the blood of the dripping. The blood that flows after the life departs.
the blood of the skin. The blood that comes out of the small blood vessels in the skin before the blood of the life departs.
one of those disqualified for the service. Such as a non-priest or a priest with a blemish.

but blood that a person disqualified for the service carried, and he returned it to a valid person who carried it. Even if the valid person returned and carried from the place where the disqualified person began to carry.
for it is impossible to fix this matter. Even though it is possible to carry the blood again by a valid person, it is impossible to cancel the carrying of the disqualified person (Lechem Mishneh).

for those disqualified for the service do not make the remaining blood leftovers. When a valid person receives the blood, the remaining blood in the animal's neck is no longer fit for the altar, and therefore if the blood spilled or was disqualified, one cannot again receive new blood from the animal's neck. But receiving of blood by a disqualified person is not considered receiving at all, and therefore blood received after it in a valid manner will be valid (see also Hilchot Me'ilah 3:2).

except for an impure person, since he is fit for the service in a sacrifice that comes in impurity etc.. A sacrifice with a fixed time is offered in impurity and by impure people when it cannot be offered in purity. Therefore, when an impure person received the blood, it is considered as if a valid person received it, and so even if the blood of the life remains, it has the law of the remaining blood that is not fit for the altar (see also ibid. 3:3).
as we have explained. Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 4:12.
an animal that is lacking any amount of its limbs. A lack that makes it blemished.
he slit its ear. He pierced it.

and in the burnt offering... and like half an olive's bulk of the sacrificial portions. In a burnt offering there is no distinction between the flesh (which in other sacrifices is eaten) and the sacrificial portions (the parts that in other sacrifices are burned), since all of it is burned.
and if he threw, it was not accepted. He did not fulfill his obligation of offering the sacrifice.

the flesh was disqualified... he should not throw the blood. And the case is where all the flesh was disqualified and not even an olive's bulk remained, but if an olive's bulk remained he should throw in the first instance (Shoham and Yishpeh).
even though the blood was thrown and the flesh is outside, the sacrifice is valid. And the flesh is permitted to be eaten (see Kesef Mishneh, Lechem Mishneh, Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 7:3).
because the flesh is destined to go out. After the blood is thrown and the sacrificial portions are burned, they eat its flesh throughout Jerusalem (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 10:5).

and throwing is effective for what went out to be burned but not for eating it. This is a separate law dealing with the disqualification of flesh that went out of the place fit for eating it (most holy offerings outside the courtyard and offerings of lesser holiness outside Jerusalem - the disqualification of "going out"), and therefore its law is to be burned and not eaten (Kesef Mishneh; and Rik"v explained that this statement refers to the preceding law, that the flesh of offerings of lesser holiness that went out at the time of the throwing outside the courtyard, the sacrifice is valid but the flesh is forbidden to eat). And even though the flesh was disqualified because it went out, the throwing of the blood is effective in that one is liable to karet for eating it if it became piggul, notar, or was eaten by impure people (as explained in the next halakhah).

and even though he did not return them, they are liable for them for piggul, notar, and impurity. Although the throwing of the blood was done when the sacrificial portions were outside, and at that time they were not fit for burning, the throwing of the blood was done properly, and therefore one is liable for eating the sacrifice if it became piggul, notar, or was eaten by impure people (see below, 18:16).
that the flesh became impure. The part of the sacrifice that is eaten.
and the fat remained intact. The fats of the sacrifice and the other parts that are burned on the altar remained pure.
for the head plate atones for the impure. It causes the impure sacrifice, which would have been disqualified and profaned, to be accepted.
sacrificial portions or limbs of a burnt offering that became impure and were burned, the head plate atones. And it is considered that they were burned properly.
as we have explained. Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 4:7.
communal offerings whose flesh and fat all became impure, he throws the blood. For communal offerings are also brought in impurity (ibid., halakhah 10).

the blood of sacrifices does not receive impurity at all etc.. Blood is considered a liquid that receives impurity and makes food susceptible to impurity (Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 1:2). But the blood of sacrifices does not receive impurity and does not make food susceptible to impurity (see also ibid. 10:16).
and blood over which the sun set and was not thrown, the sacrifice is disqualified. See also Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 4:1.
all the bloods that are given on the outer altar. The blood of all sacrifices (except the burned sin offerings, whose law will be explained below, halakhah 3).

if he gave them one application only, he atoned. And in the first instance one must apply on the altar four applications from the blood of a sin offering; two applications from the blood of a burnt offering, guilt offering, and peace offering; and one application from the blood of a firstborn, tithe, and Passover offering.
and the blood of your sacrifices shall be poured out. One pouring.

those given by throwing. The burnt offering, guilt offering, and peace offerings, whose blood is given on the altar in a manner in which the priest stands at a distance from the altar and throws the blood from the vessel against the wall of the altar.
that he gave by pouring. When the priest stands near the altar and pours the blood directly onto the base (as is to be done for a firstborn, tithe, and Passover offering).
all the bloods that are given on the inner altar. For details see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 1:15-16.

if he left out one of them, he did not atone. If he did not sprinkle all of the sprinklings (see there 5:12-13 for where their blood is sprinkled; and pouring the remainder of the blood onto the base after finishing the sprinklings is not indispensable - there 19:4).

a sin offering from which he gave one application and the owners died etc.. It is forbidden to offer a sin offering whose owners died (below, 4:1); however, after he sprinkled one application the owners were atoned for, and he may complete the sprinklings.

he gave the one by day, he shall not give the three at night. For the other sprinklings too (which are not indispensable) are considered valid sprinklings, and one may not sprinkle from the blood of sacrifices at night (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 4:1).

and if he gave one inside and completed them outside, he is liable. To karet, for the other sprinklings too are considered valid sprinklings, and one who sprinkles from blood fit for the altar is liable (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 19:3).
if he was sprinkling and the hand of the sprinkler was cut off... the sprinkling did not count for him. Since the one giving became blemished (Rashi, Zevachim 15a).

he changed the giving on the corners. He changed the manner of giving the blood. For with a sin offering he gave with a vessel and not with his hand, and with other sacrifices he gave with his hand and not with a vessel.

from the corner and inward. The corner is the angle of the altar corresponding to the projection at its top. And "from the corner and inward" means in the continuation of the altar wall beyond the corner's boundary (Mirkevet HaMishneh, Har HaMoriah). On the outer altar it means beyond the cubit adjacent to the angle (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 5:7).
and likewise in other sacrifices. For in other sacrifices too the blood must be given on the corner of the altar (see there 5:6).
blood that it is a commandment to give above. A sin offering.
from the half of the altar. The height of the altar is divided in two by the red line (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 2:9).
that it is a commandment to give below. Such as a burnt offering, guilt offering, and peace offering.
that it is a commandment to give inside in the Sanctuary. The burned sin offerings.

on the ramp, not opposite the base. He gave the blood on the ramp far from the altar, and not on the two cubits at the end of the ramp adjacent to the altar, which were above the surrounding ledge and above the place of the base (Melechet Shlomo, Zevachim 3:2).
the flesh of the sacrifice is disqualified. The flesh is burned and not eaten, and the sacrificial portions are not burned on the altar (Or Sameach, Likkutei Halachot Zevachim 26b).
when this thrower was valid for the service. Then if he threw improperly, the sacrifice is disqualified, and even if the blood of the life remains, it cannot be received again.

the flesh of the sacrifice is not disqualified if the blood of the life remains etc.. A disqualified person's throwing not in its place is not considered a throwing and does not disqualify the sacrifice, and therefore if the blood of the life remains, a valid priest can receive the blood and atone (but when a disqualified person threw the blood in its place, the sacrifice is entirely disqualified - Mirkevet HaMishneh, above 1:28).
blood in blood. The blood of two sacrifices mixed in one vessel.
a cup among cups. The blood of each sacrifice is in a separate vessel, but it is not known to which sacrifice each vessel belongs.
those given in four applications among those given in four applications. The blood of one animal sin offering mixed with the blood of another animal sin offering (Lechem Mishneh).
those given in one application mixed with those given in two that are like four, he shall give it all in one application. For after the fact one application atones.

everything is poured into the drain. The water channel into which the blood in the courtyard drained, for it is impossible to throw the blood, since one may not give above what is given below, and one may not give below what is given above.
and the sacrifices are disqualified. For the blood never reached the altar at all.
even if the remainders of a sin offering were mixed. Which are poured onto the base.
with the blood of a burnt offering. Which is thrown against the wall of the altar.
and if he did not ask. The priest, what to do with the mixture.
he gave from the mixture above and below, it is valid. Although it is forbidden to give the blood not in its place, since he gave above and below, both are valid.

even an individual's sin offering that is eaten is forbidden, as it is said, "and any sin offering from whose blood is brought" etc.. Although the plain sense of the verse speaks of the burned sin offerings, whose blood must be given inside and whose flesh is burned, the Sages learned that even a sin offering that is eaten, whose blood must be given outside, if its blood entered inside, it becomes forbidden and its law is to be burned (see Ramban, Leviticus 6:23).
by way of entry. In the usual manner in which people enter.
through the wicket. A small gate at the side of the great gate of the Sanctuary, through which one can enter the Sanctuary from the side (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 4:6).
whose blood enters the Sanctuary. For sprinkling opposite the curtain and on the golden altar.
for this place inward is their place. And any sin offering whose blood was brought in further than the place to which it should be brought is disqualified.
the bull and the goat of Yom Kippur, whose blood enters the Holy of Holies. To sprinkle from their blood between the staves of the Ark.
if he brought their blood into the Holy of Holies and sprinkled from it. And did not finish the sprinklings that must be sprinkled there.

and took it out to the Sanctuary and brought it back into the Holy of Holies, it is disqualified. For its entry is considered an entry inward and disqualifies the blood (Mirkevet HaMishneh; and the Ra'avad explained the Rambam differently and therefore objected to him).
for once the blood went out of its place, it is disqualified. Since the blood left the Sanctuary, it is disqualified if it enters it again.
a sin offering whose blood he received in two cups. And both are fit to be thrown on the altar.
and one of them went outside. And became disqualified (above, 1:35).
the blood of the sin offering. The outer one.
that he brought in to atone with it inside. To sprinkle from it.
he brought the sin offering itself into the Sanctuary. After its slaughter, even before the receiving of the blood (Rik"v).

he brought the blood of a bird sin offering into the Sanctuary in its neck etc.. The blood of a bird sin offering is given directly from the bird's neck to the altar without a vessel. Therefore when the priest brings the bird into the Sanctuary with the blood in its neck, there is doubt whether this entry is considered bringing blood in a vessel, which disqualifies the sacrifice, or not (and it is unlike the previous halakhah, where the bird convulsed and entered on its own, and then certainly it is not considered as brought in a vessel). Some explain that the case here is where he cut the neck from the body of the bird and brought it in, but if he brought in the whole bird with its blood, it has the law of the bird sin offering that convulsed, and is valid (Aruch HaShulchan 128:6).

there is doubt whether the vessel disqualifies its blood or does not disqualify. In this case he cannot give the blood on the altar directly from the neck but from a vessel into which he collected the blood, and there is doubt whether the blood of a bird sin offering may be given in a vessel or not.
the remainders of all four are poured on the base. The blood in all the cups was used for sprinkling, and therefore all of it is considered remainders that must be poured on the base.

and the other cups are poured into the drain. The blood in them did not atone on the altar, so there is no commandment to pour it on the base, but it is drained with the rest of the blood into the water channel in the Temple.

he shall not sprinkle from it, and if he sprinkled it is invalid. For every drop of blood that reaches water is nullified in it, and therefore even if a large amount of blood was poured onto a small amount of water, it is invalid (Babylonian Talmud, Zevachim 78a; for this principle see Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 16:28; Hilchot Tum'at Met 2:14).
if it has the appearance of blood. The blood remained in its redness and its color was not weakened (Commentary on the Mishnah, Zevachim 8:6).
wine or unconsecrated blood fell into it. Which do not change the color of the blood.
we estimate them as if they were water etc.. We estimate how they would have affected the appearance of the blood had they been water.
those unfit for the altar. That are not fit for offering at all, such as blemished animals.
sacrifices that were disqualified in their slaughter. That were fit for offering and were disqualified at the time of slaughter.

and even if all the cups were offered except one. When the valid blood and the disqualified blood are in separate cups that became mixed, and it is not known which blood is in which cup, even if he threw all the cups except one, we do not say that the disqualified blood was probably already thrown, but rather we pour out the blood of the last cup.
and all those sacrifices are disqualified. Lest their blood was poured and not thrown.
it was mixed with the blood of the dripping. The blood of the life was mixed with the blood that flows after the life departs, which is disqualified for offering (above, 1:26).

and if he did not ask and gave, it is valid. If he gave the mixture of the blood of the life and the dripping, it is valid, but if he gave from the mixture of the blood of sacrifices and the blood of disqualified ones, it is invalid (Rik"v and others). Some wrote that even when he gave from the mixture of sacrifices and disqualified ones it is valid (Har HaMoriah, Aruch HaShulchan 128:15-16 and others).
and the handfuls and the frankincense. That are burned from the meal offerings.
and the meal offerings that are burned. Such as the meal offering of priests and meal offerings accompanying libations.
after they were sanctified in a service vessel. But handfuls and meal offerings that were not sanctified in a vessel are invalid.

whether by hand or in a vessel. And in the first instance one should burn the limbs by hand (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 6:4), and the meal offerings, handfuls, and frankincense from a vessel (ibid. 13:12).
whether with the right or with the left. But the other services are valid only with the right (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 5:18).
in the hin. A liquid-measuring vessel (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 1:17).
limbs that he arranged. On the top of the altar, not on the fire.
and if he did so, it was accepted. The sacrifice went up for acceptance and they fulfilled their obligation of offering it.
most holy offerings. Whose slaughter place in the courtyard is north of the altar (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:15-16).
and he brings down the entrails and rinses them below. Like other burnt offerings, as detailed in Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 6:6.
and he takes down the skin and gives it to the priests. After the offering of the flesh, like other burnt offerings (ibid. 5:19).
and likewise slaughtered sacrifices. Such as peace offerings.
and he again burns the rest. The sacrificial portions that remained on top of the altar.
for anything fit for the fires. Things that are burned on the altar, such as sacrificial portions and the handful of a meal offering.
a burnt offering that he brought up alive to the top of the altar shall come down. And one does not slaughter it on the altar.
and likewise the handful of a meal offering that was not sanctified in a service vessel. Since he did not yet separate the handful from the meal offering, it is not yet fit for the altar fire.
things forbidden for the altar. Such as a bestiality victim and one who committed bestiality, an animal worshiped, and one set aside for idolatry (see Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 3:11).
because they were not fit from the beginning. From the outset they were not fit to be offered on the altar.
our sacrifices. Which a night passed over and were disqualified.
for the blood spent the night. The blood was already disqualified at sunset.
the flesh. The flesh of the burnt offering, which has the law of the sacrificial portions.
the sacrificial portions. They must be offered during the night (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 4:2), and at the end of the night they are disqualified.
that was disqualified by a thought of time or by a thought of place. He thought during his service to offer it or eat it after the proper time or outside the proper place.
by a thought of changing. He offered the sacrifice for the sake of another sacrifice (such as a burnt offering for a peace offering) or not for its owner.

that impure people received and threw its blood, since etc.. Communal offerings are offered by impure people when most of the priests are impure (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 4:12), and therefore when impure people served, the sacrifice was not rejected if it went up on the altar. But if other disqualified people received or threw the blood, the sacrifice is entirely disqualified.
and whose blood was given outside its place. The blood was not thrown in its proper place on the altar (see above, 2:10).
anything whose disqualification occurred in the sanctuary. That was fit from the beginning for the altar, and was disqualified afterward.

if they came down, they shall not go up a second time etc.. Although they should be burned while they are on the altar, their disqualification was not nullified and they should not be brought up in the first instance.
and if the fire took hold of them. If the disqualified items came down from the altar after being burned and the altar fire had taken hold of them.
they shall go up a second time and he completes their burning. For after the altar fire took hold of them they became the altar's, and therefore one must complete their burning even if they fell off.
a handful that became piggul. And its law is that if it went up, it shall not come down.

and part of it on the ground and part of it the fire took hold of, all of it goes up. The entire handful is considered one unit, and just as a disqualified limb that the fire took hold of must be brought up and burned, so a disqualified handful (whose parts are separate) of which the fire took hold of part must be brought up (Babylonian Talmud, Zevachim 43b).
limbs. Of burnt offerings that must be burned.
and fats. The sacrificial portions of offerings that are eaten.
and handfuls. The part of the meal offering that is burned.

as if they had spent the night in the courtyard etc.. And they were disqualified by spending the night. Therefore if they came down they shall not go up, but as long as they are on the altar he may burn them.

and the airspace of the altar is like the altar. Disqualified items that reached the airspace of the altar, even if they did not rest on it, have the law of those placed on the altar and one should not take them down.

and sacrificial portions of offerings of lesser holiness that he brought up before the throwing of the blood etc.. Although before the throwing of the blood the sacrificial portions are not fit for burning, they should not be taken down.
the bread of the altar. They belong to the altar fire.

he separated two guilt offerings as a backup. He was obligated to bring a guilt offering (or a sin offering, Rashi, Me'ilah 7b) and separated two animals so that if one is lost he will be atoned for with the other.

and slaughtered both of them etc.. In this case the guilt offering whose blood was thrown first on the altar atones for him, and the second guilt offering is disqualified (see below, 4:5). And if he brought up the sacrificial portions of the second guilt offering, they come down (Rik"v, Kesef Mishneh, and similar to the opinion of the Ra'avad in his critical notes).

and the libations shall come down. The wine libations that are poured on the altar come down, since they are not placed on the fire but go down to the drains (and even in a case where the sacrifice was disqualified and its libations were not disqualified, the libations come down - Rik"v, Kesef Mishneh).
libations that come on their own. For example, where one brings wine for libation without a sacrifice.

even though this one is disqualified and that one is disqualified, this one is as if it had not been sanctified at all. The handful is sanctified by its taking and placing in a service vessel, and when it was taken by a non-priest, it is as if it was not sanctified at all, and even if it went up it comes down (above, halakhah 5). By contrast, pinching a bird's neck by a non-priest, although it is not valid and disqualifies the sacrifice, is considered pinching (see below, 7:1).
and the non-priest and the other disqualified people are the same. Their law is equal to what is stated here.
anything not fit for the fires. That is not fit at all to be burned on the altar.
the flesh of most holy offerings... and the showbread. All of these are eaten and are not burned on the altar.
and the incense. It is not burned on the outer altar.

and the wool on the heads of lambs etc.. When they are attached to the flesh of the burnt offering they must be burned (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 6:2), but when not attached they are not to be brought up, and if one brought them up they must be taken down.
a handful whose oil dripped onto a bone. Oil from the handful of the meal offering that was squeezed onto a bone that is not attached, and without the oil it should not be brought up and burned.

he should return it, for the matter is in doubt, since perhaps things attached to what goes up are considered as going up. There is doubt whether something attached to something that goes up to the altar is drawn after it and also has the law of going up. And out of doubt, one should bring the bone up to the altar so as not to treat sacred things with disrespect by leaving them below (Kesef Mishneh).
the inner altar sanctifies disqualified items, whether they are fit for it or not fit for it. Even things fit only for the outer altar and not for the inner are sanctified if they go up on it.
foreign incense went up on it. All incense that goes up on the outer altar is foreign, since it is not fit for burning there (Rik"v).
but the inner altar, onto which a handful of a meal offering went up... shall not come down. Even though the inner altar is used only for burning incense and not for burning other things.
and once something fit for it reaches the ramp. Things fit to be brought up to the altar.
once something fit for it reaches the vessel. A liquid in a vessel that holds liquids, and a solid in a vessel that holds dry things, as explained in the next halakhah.

and it is never redeemed even though it was disqualified, as we have explained in the laws of things forbidden for the altar. For valid things fit for the altar are not redeemed at all, and if they were disqualified they can be redeemed only until they enter a service vessel (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 6:4-5).
in the liquid and dry measures that were in the Temple. Measuring vessels, which are specific for liquids or dry things.
as we have explained in the laws of the Temple vessels. 1:16-17.

but the basins sanctify the liquid and the dry. The vessels in which blood is received, which although they are generally used for liquids can also be used for dry things, for the princes brought fine flour for a meal offering in them (Babylonian Talmud, Zevachim 88a).
and service vessels sanctify blood that is disqualified from being offered. And one throws it on the altar even though it is disqualified.
and they sanctify only with intent. That he intends to sanctify what he puts into them.
and they sanctify only from their inside. And not from their outside.
if they perform something of their function that they used to perform and they are whole. If they are now fit for use as they were before they were pierced.

but the measures do not sanctify when they are lacking, unless his intention is to fill them. Measuring vessels do not sanctify when they are lacking, unless his intention is to fill them completely, in which case they immediately sanctify what he began to put into them even if he has not yet finished filling them (and see the commentators who discussed the relationship between the law of measuring vessels and other service vessels).

and if his intention is not to fill them, they sanctify to be disqualified but not to be offered. When he does not intend to fill the measuring vessel completely, they do not sanctify what was put into them so that it may be offered, but they sanctify it with the sanctity of the body so that it can become disqualified in the way sacrifices become disqualified, such as by contact with impurity, spending the night, and going out of the courtyard.

who took a handful of a meal offering at night and put its handful into a service vessel, it is burned. Since taking a handful at night is invalid and disqualifies the meal offering (Babylonian Talmud, Menachot 100a).

an altar that was damaged. The measure of damage to the structure of the altar is a handbreadth (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 2:18), and to the stones of the altar, enough to catch a fingernail (ibid. 1:14).

all the sacrifices that were slaughtered there in the Temple were disqualified. And since they were disqualified, they are rejected from being offered even after the altar is repaired ("what was fit and was rejected does not become fit again" - Aruch HaShulchan 130:22, and see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 15:4 for explanation).

for living creatures are not rejected. Living creatures that were fit for a sacrifice and became disqualified are never disqualified permanently, and if they become fit again, they are valid for offering (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot there).
he consecrated animals before the altar was built. When the altar was damaged.

for what was rejected from the start is not rejected. Something that from the time of its consecration was not fit for offering, when it becomes fit is valid for offering (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot there, below 4:24).

they do not eat sacrifices while the altar is damaged... until it is built. In this case the sacrifices were not disqualified from being eaten, but the place is not fit for eating sacrifices, and therefore after the altar is repaired they can be eaten again (see Likkutei Halachot, Zevachim 59a).
the offspring of a sin offering. That was born to a sin offering that became pregnant after it was separated (and for when it was separated while pregnant, see below, 5:6).

and the substitute for a sin offering. He said of an unconsecrated animal that it should be sacred in place of the consecrated animal. The law is that the consecrated animal remains in its sanctity and the second animal also becomes sacred (Hilchot Temurah 2:1).

and a sin offering that was lost and found after the owners were atoned for. That after the sin offering was lost the owners separated another sin offering and offered it, and afterward the first sin offering was found.
or it shall graze until it has a blemish. And after it has a blemish it is redeemed.
therefore it shall die. Because of the doubt it cannot be redeemed.
not that he should kill them with a vessel or with his hand. Because of its sanctity one should not kill it with one's hands.
he should put them into a house. Without food.
and all these matters were heard from the mouth of Moses our teacher. The law of sin offerings that must die was learned by tradition from Moses our teacher.

whether it is fit or not fit, it shall graze etc.. Even if the animal is still fit to be a sin offering, one does not offer it as another communal sin offering, but after it has a blemish one brings a burnt offering with its proceeds (below, 5:2).
and let their proceeds fall to the freewill offerings. For the needs of freewill burnt offerings, as explained below, halakhah 11.

and the community does not make a substitute, as will be explained. Hilchot Temurah 1:1. Likewise all of Israel does not die (Babylonian Talmud, Temurah 16a; and in printed editions these words were added into the Rambam's text).

the bull and goat of Yom Kippur... and likewise the goats of idolatry. All of these are communal sin offerings that are burned (and the same applies to the bull for a communal unwitting error in a ruling, Rik"v).
that were lost, and he separated others in their place. And after the others that he separated were offered, he found the sin offerings that had been lost.
and why should they not be offered themselves as a freewill offering, since they are males. And they are themselves fit for a burnt offering.

a decree lest one offer after atonement because of before atonement. For if they were found before the owners were atoned for with others, they are still fit as a sin offering (see the next halakhah).

he drew one of the two and was atoned for with it, the other shall die. For since he was atoned for with one of them, the law of the other becomes that of a sin offering that was lost and whose owners were atoned for with another.
he came to take counsel. To ask which animal to offer.
they tell him that he should be atoned for with the one he separated first. Since he consecrated it first for the sacrifice, it is proper that he offer it (Aruch HaShulchan 131:17).

and the second shall graze until it has a blemish and its proceeds fall to the freewill offerings. Since he took counsel, their law is like one who separated two sin offerings as a backup, where he is atoned for with one and the other grazes (below, halakhah 5).
and a blemished one shall be redeemed. And its proceeds fall to the freewill offerings.
a blemished one was slaughtered. After it had been redeemed.

before the blood of the unblemished one was thrown, it is forbidden for benefit. When two sin offerings stand and the owner drew one of them and offered it, the law of the other is to die. And the blemished sin offering becomes forbidden even if it was already slaughtered at the time the blood was thrown, and all the more so if it was still alive (Rik"v; and some emended and wrote that if the blemished animal was slaughtered before the throwing, its flesh is permitted, and only if the animal was alive at the time of the throwing and was slaughtered afterward is its flesh forbidden - Kesef Mishneh and Lechem Mishneh).

he was atoned for with the first, the second dies and the third grazes. When he took the first (and did not take counsel), the law of the second is to die like a sin offering whose owners were atoned for with another. But the third was not brought in place of the first but in place of the second, which was not offered, and therefore its law is not to die.
he was atoned for with the middle one, both of them die. For it came in place of both of them.
two sin offerings as a backup. So that if one dies or is disqualified, he will be atoned for with the other.
and its year passed. An individual's sin offering is valid only in its first year.

even though it was found blemished or was found after its year passed, it does not die. Its law is not to die (except in a case where he drew one and offered it without taking counsel, in which case it dies even if it was found before atonement, as above, halakhah 3).

the main loss of it was at night. The beginning of its loss was at night, and since this hour is not fit for atonement (for offering the sin offering), loss at this time is not considered a loss (Babylonian Talmud, Temurah 22b).
the shepherd. The one appointed to guard it.

and let their proceeds fall to the freewill offerings. They put the money into one of the chests ("shofarot") in the Temple from which they buy communal freewill burnt offerings (see Hilchot Shekalim 2:2-3).
and another recognizes it even at the end of the world. One person knows where it is.
in a hidden place on the step. In a place hidden from view.
they offer it on the presumption that he is alive. And we do not worry that he died and the law of his sin offering is to die (for a similar law see Hilchot Gerushin 6:28).

in the case of a bird sin offering, or the animal sin offering of a woman who is not subject to laying on of hands. Since every man must lay hands in the courtyard on the animal sacrifices he brings (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 3:6), they would not accept animal sacrifices of people from overseas through an agent. But the offerings of women and birds, which do not require laying on of hands (ibid., halakhot 7-8), they would accept through an agent (see also below, 6:4).
a definite guilt offering. That is brought for certain transgressions that he definitely committed.
and its owners were atoned for. With another animal.
for whatever in a sin offering dies, in a guilt offering grazes. In all cases where the law for a sin offering is death, the law for a guilt offering is grazing.
that was released to graze. That was uprooted from its original designation as a guilt offering, and it was determined that it shall graze until it has a blemish.
a decree lest one offer after atonement because of before atonement. See above, halakhah 2.
one who separates a female for his guilt offering. A guilt offering is brought only from male sheep.
and if he offered his guilt offering. And there is no longer any need for the proceeds of the first one to bring the guilt offering.
and likewise its offspring. The offspring of the female that was separated for a guilt offering shall graze until it has a blemish, and its proceeds fall to the freewill offerings.

he separated a female for his burnt offering. An animal burnt offering comes only from males, and since it cannot be offered, they sell it and bring a burnt offering with its proceeds (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 15:5).

it shall graze until it has a blemish and he shall bring a burnt offering with its proceeds. The offspring became sacred through its mother, and since she is not fit to be offered, they do not offer it either. And when it has a blemish he brings a burnt offering with its proceeds (and its proceeds do not fall to the freewill offerings), an individual's burnt offering.
a commoner who separated a male for his sin offering. A sin offering of an individual, any person, comes as a female.
and a prince who separated a female goat for his sin offering. The individual sin offering of a prince (a king) comes as a male.
and an anointed priest who separated a cow for his sin offering. Instead of bringing a bull as he is obligated.
these do not become sanctified. Since they are not fit for the sin offering for which they were consecrated, no sanctity takes hold of them at all (see also Hilchot Temurah 1:21).
neither the sanctity of the body. The sanctity of a sacrifice, which must be offered on the altar and cannot be redeemed unless it has a blemish.
nor the sanctity of value. The sanctity of property consecrated for Temple maintenance.
they shall be sold unblemished. And there is no sanctity at all on their proceeds.
a suspensive guilt offering. One who is in doubt whether he committed a transgression for which a sin offering is owed brings a suspensive guilt offering (Hilchot Shegagot 8:1).
and it became known to him that he did not sin. And he is exempt.
or that he definitely sinned. And he is liable for a sin offering and not a guilt offering.

it shall graze until it has a blemish and its proceeds fall to the freewill offerings, because his heart etc.. Although it became clear that he was not obligated in a guilt offering at all, sanctity took hold of the animal because a person who consecrates a suspensive guilt offering intends to consecrate it even if he did not sin in this sin, as atonement for one of his transgressions. But he cannot offer it as a suspensive guilt offering because he is not obligated in it, and therefore its proceeds fall to the freewill offerings.

even if he separated it on the testimony of witnesses and they were found to be false witnesses, its proceeds fall to the freewill offerings. Even when they obligated him to separate a guilt offering against his will, on the basis of testimony, and the witnesses were found to be liars, sanctity took hold of the guilt offering, for even in such a case the one who separates intends to separate as atonement for one of his transgressions.
the blood shall be poured out. Into the drain, and it is not thrown on the altar.
and the flesh shall be burned like the rest of the disqualified consecrated animals. Below, 19:1.

it became known to him after the blood was thrown, the flesh is eaten by the priests like all guilt offerings. Since at the time the blood was thrown he was obligated in a suspensive guilt offering (for he was still in doubt whether he had sinned or not), the guilt offering is valid and its flesh is eaten.

if before it was slaughtered it became known to him that he did not sin etc.. The consecration was made only with the intention of atoning for the sin that was committed, and when it became clear that he did not sin, the consecration was entirely nullified.
and if after it was slaughtered, it shall be buried. Like unconsecrated animals slaughtered in the courtyard (below, 19:11).
and if after the blood was thrown. It became known that he did not sin.

the flesh shall go out to the place of burning like the rest of the disqualified consecrated animals. Although it is unconsecrated meat slaughtered in the courtyard, it should not be buried because it looks like consecrated animals that were disqualified (Babylonian Talmud, Keritot 24b).
and he separated two as a backup. So that if one is lost he will be atoned for with the other.
and it goes without saying in a definite one that this is so. Similar to a sin offering (above, halakhah 5).

all the guilt offerings in the Torah. The guilt offering for robbery, the guilt offering for misappropriation, the guilt offering for a betrothed maidservant (Hilchot Shegagot 9:1), and the suspensive guilt offering (ibid. 8:1).
come as two-year-olds. A male lamb in its second year (a ram).
and they come with the silver of shekels. That they be worth at least two shekels (sela'im).
and there is no set amount for their price. There is no fixed sum for their cost.
a suspensive guilt offering is explicitly from the larger ones. It is stated explicitly in the Torah that it is a ram (Leviticus 5:18).

and from the oral tradition they learned that it comes only with the silver of shekels. For it says of it "according to your valuation," as is said of the guilt offering for misappropriation, in which it is explicit that it is with the silver of shekels (Commentary on the Mishnah, Keritot 6:6).
and at the time of atonement, worth two is valid. For the value of the guilt offering is determined at the time it is offered.

for what is rejected from the start is not rejected, and it has not yet been fit etc.. Since from the time of its separation the guilt offering was not fit for a sacrifice, when its price rises and it becomes fit for a sacrifice, it is valid (see also above, 3:24).

and even though it increased in value on its own, a person is atoned for with the improvement of consecrated property. Although the guilt offering doubled in price after it was consecrated and the owners benefit from its improvement, it is permitted to offer it and be atoned for with it.

for living creatures are not rejected, as we have explained. Although the guilt offering was valid and was later disqualified ("was fit and was rejected"), since it is a living animal, it is not disqualified by its rejection (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 15:4).
for a blemish that fell and passed. An animal that was disqualified because of a blemish and afterward the blemish healed, it is valid.
if one of them was worth two selas. Its price rose or the seller sold it to him cheaply.
and the second shall graze until it has a blemish and its proceeds fall to the freewill offerings. Since it was bought with guilt offering money and cannot be offered (for the other ram was offered).

lacking time in the owners. At a time when the owners are not yet fit to offer the sacrifice (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 18:9), such as a nazirite or a leper who have not completed their purification.
and its form shall pass and it shall go out to the place of burning. One must wait until it spoils and its form changes, and then burn it.
except for a guilt offering that he slaughtered not for its own sake. He slaughtered it for the sake of another sacrifice or for the sake of one who is not its owner.
for it is valid, as will be explained. Below, 15:1; whereas a sin offering slaughtered not for its own sake is invalid.

the burnt offering of a nazirite, the burnt offering of a woman who gave birth, the burnt offering of a leper. These obligatory burnt offerings are brought specifically from a lamb in its first year (Hilchot Nezirut 8:1, Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:3), unlike a freewill burnt offering, which comes from males of all kinds and all sizes.
lacking time in the owners. Before the completion of the nazirite period or the completion of the purification of the woman who gave birth or the leper.
valid. Although they did not fulfill their obligation with them (Tosefta, Zevachim 1:3).
and they require libations. Even though they did not offer them properly, they were not exempted from the libations that are brought with every animal burnt offering (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 2:2).
anything that does not disqualify a freewill burnt offering. The age of the animal and lack of time in the owners.
whether it was accepted for the owners or whether it was not accepted for them. Whether the owners fulfilled their obligation with the sacrifice or did not.

one who separated money for his sin offering and died etc.. Money that was separated for a sin offering has the law of the sin offering itself, and therefore when the law of the sin offering is death (see above, 4:1), the law of the money is to be lost.
the money shall go to the Dead Sea. To a place where the money will be lost and will bring no benefit (and the Dead Sea is the Great Sea - Hilchot Arachin VaCharamin 8:8 according to accurate texts).

he shall bring a sin offering from this and that and the rest shall fall to the freewill offerings. The remaining money has the law of "leftover of a sin offering," which falls to the freewill offerings (below, halakhah 9). However, if he drew the money of one of the separations in order to be atoned for with it, the other money goes to the Dead Sea (Commentary on the Mishnah, Temurah 4:3, Rik"v and Lechem Mishneh based on Babylonian Talmud, Temurah 22b; and compare above, 4:3).
he separated two groups of money as a backup. So that if one is lost he will be atoned for with the other (see above, 4:5).
these are unconsecrated and did not become sanctified. For he is not obligated in a sin offering.
and thinking that he is liable for two. He thought that he had committed two transgressions for which a sin offering is owed.

and the rest shall fall to the freewill offerings. The rest of the money that he separated falls to the freewill offerings, because he was obligated in a sin offering, so their separation is not considered a consecration made in error, and they have the law of the leftover of a sin offering (Rik"v); and likewise when he separated two animals, the second animal shall graze and its proceeds fall to the freewill offerings (Kesef Mishneh).
for the matter is all the more so for other sacrifices, where the leftover is unconsecrated. For their sanctity is lighter than the sanctity of a sin offering (Rik"v).

the leftover is unconsecrated. Since he said "I will bring from them," he did not consecrate all of them. But if he said "these are," the leftover falls to the freewill offerings like the leftover of a sin offering (Rik"v, Har HaMoriah).

for a sinner's meal offering. Which a poor person brings who is obligated in a burnt-or-sliding-scale offering (see below, halakhah 9), and the meal offering of a suspected adulteress (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 12:4).
and he brought his meal offering from them. And money remained.
who separated a sinner's meal offering and some remained. Fine flour remained.

the leftover shall come as a freewill meal offering. The leftover of a sin offering falls to the freewill offerings. However, since there is no communal freewill meal offering, one brings from the leftover an individual's freewill meal offering (Or Sameach).
the tenth of an ephah of the High Priest. An obligatory meal offering that the High Priest brings every day (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 3:18).
and the leftover of the price of its libations. What remains of the money he separated to buy wine for libation together with the nazirite's offerings.
we have already explained in Shekalim. Hilchot Shekalim 3:13.
that the leftover of the shekels is unconsecrated. When he separates or collects for the half-shekel more than is needed.
the nests of zavim, the nests of zavot, the nests of women who gave birth. Bird offerings brought to complete the purification process of a zav, a zavah, and a woman who gave birth.
their leftovers shall fall to the freewill offerings and be offered as burnt offerings, as we have explained. Hilchot Shekalim 2:2-3.
the leftover of a burnt offering for a burnt offering. If he separated money for a burnt offering and some remained, they buy another burnt offering with the remainder.

the leftover of a Passover offering for peace offerings. With the money that remained from the money he consecrated for the Passover offering, they buy a peace offering, since another Passover offering cannot be bought with it, and both peace offerings and the Passover offering are offerings of lesser holiness (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shekalim 2:5; and see also Hilchot Korban Pesach 4:10).
the leftover of nazirites for nazirites. A person who separated money for offerings for several nazirites, other nazirites will be atoned for with the money that remained (Hilchot Nezirut 9:1).

the leftover of a nazirite for that same nazirite. The commentators found this law difficult, since elsewhere in the Rambam (Hilchot Shekalim 2:2, and see Hilchot Nezirut 9:1) it is explicit that the leftover of a nazirite goes to the freewill offerings (see Rik"v, Har HaMoriah, Ma'aseh Rokeach; and Tzafnat Pane'ach on Hilchot Nezirut there).
in a fixed sin offering. A sin offering that always comes from an animal.

in a burnt-or-sliding-scale offering. A sin offering that comes in certain cases and varies according to a person's financial situation: a rich person brings an animal offering, a poor person brings a bird offering, and one who cannot afford even birds brings a meal offering (Hilchot Shegagot 10:1-4).

he brings a bird in their place and redeems them for the bird, and benefits from them. Instead of buying an animal with the money he separated, he redeems it for a bird, and the money that remains goes out to unconsecrated status and he may use it for his needs (see also ibid. 10:10).
he separated an animal and it developed a blemish. He separated an animal when he was rich, and now he is poor and brings a bird offering (see also Hilchot Shegagot 10:11).
it shall be sold and he shall bring a bird with its proceeds. And the money that remains he may use for his needs.
he separated a bird and it was disqualified. For example, it became missing a limb.
for a bird has no redemption, as we have explained in the laws of things forbidden for the altar. Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 6:4.
those obligated in nests. Those obligated to bring two birds, one for a burnt offering and one for a sin offering.

even if he said, "This is the money of my sin offering and this is the money of my burnt offering". After he separated the money for his nest without specification, he later specified that part of the money would be for the burnt offering and part for the sin offering (Har HaMoriah).
he may mix the money. He is permitted to mix them.

for nests are not specified except by the owners' taking or the priest's performance. The designation of the birds of the nest as burnt offering and sin offering is made at the time the owners buy the birds. And if they did not specify at the time of purchase, they cannot determine which is for the sin offering and which is for the burnt offering, and the matter is determined only when the priest actually offers them (see also below, 8:8). Likewise the money intended for a nest can be designated only at the time of separation and not afterward.

all that unspecified money shall fall to the freewill offerings etc.. Like the money of a burnt offering, which when its owners die is used to bring a burnt offering, and not like the money of a sin offering, which when its owners die is taken to the Dead Sea.
and he said, "I take upon myself a burnt offering". A freewill burnt offering, and now he is obligated in a sin offering and a burnt offering.

he died and left the money, it shall go to the Dead Sea. Because of the concern that his intention was to bring a sin offering from it, and the money of a sin offering whose owners died goes to the Dead Sea (Lechem Mishneh).
from the sin offerings that die. Above, 4:1.
an ox that is stoned. An ox whose law is to be stoned (for example, one that killed a person) and which is forbidden for benefit (Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 4:22).
even one in ten thousand. A sin offering that must die or an ox that is stoned, which became mixed with ten thousand oxen of the Temple treasury.

because living creatures are significant and are not nullified. Unlike ordinary forbidden items, which are nullified in a minority when mixed with permitted ones, living creatures are not nullified in any proportion (see also Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 16:7).
and if he offered, it was accepted. Even if he offered only one animal, for we follow the valid majority and not the invalid individual (Aruch HaShulchan 135:5).

for living creatures are not rejected. Although when it was mixed it was disqualified from being offered in the first instance, it is not entirely rejected, and after the fact, if they offered it, it is valid (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 15:4).
from things forbidden for the altar. Such as a harlot's fee and a dog's price (for the list of prohibited items see Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 3:11).
all of them shall graze until they have a blemish etc.. Since they are not nullified, it is impossible to offer them, and they must be redeemed after they have a blemish.

and he shall bring with the price of the best of them from the kind of consecrated animals that was mixed. When one consecrated animal became mixed in a mixture of animals that include animals forbidden for the altar, one must buy with the redemption money another animal that will be offered in its place. And since it is not known which animal was the consecrated one, one must buy an animal equal to the best animal in the mixture, and the rest of the money is unconsecrated (and likewise when one forbidden animal became mixed with several consecrated animals, one must buy with the price of the best ones the same number of offerings as were in the mixture, and the price of the worst animal is unconsecrated, Lechem Mishneh).
consecrated animals mixed with unconsecrated unblemished ones. Consecrated animals became mixed with unconsecrated unblemished animals that are fit to be consecrated for the altar.

the unconsecrated animals in the mixture shall be sold for the needs of that kind. They sell the unconsecrated animals in the mixture (wherever they are) to people who need to bring an offering of the kind of offering that became mixed with these animals, and they offer the entire mixture.
and the money is unconsecrated for all purposes, since it is the price of unconsecrated animals. Which was given in exchange for the unconsecrated animals in the mixture.

consecrated animals among consecrated animals, kind with its own kind. The offering of one person with the offering of another person, and both of the same kind (such as a burnt offering with a burnt offering and the like).
this one shall be offered for its owners and that one shall be offered for its owners etc.. The priest thinks at the time of offering that each sacrifice is for its owner.
in the offerings of women, which have no laying on of hands. And therefore there is no need to know who the owner is (see also above, 4:14).
since each one must lay hands on the head of his sacrifice. And it is impossible for the owners to appoint an agent for this (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 3:8).

until one gives his portion to his fellow. Each one will transfer to the other his portion in one of the sacrifices (if this sacrifice is his), and thereby he will certainly be the owner of the sacrifice and will be able to lay hands on it.
and each one shall bring with the price of the best of them of that kind. Each one shall bring an offering at the price of the offering that was sold at a higher price, lest that was his offering.

they shall not be offered even like the stricter of them. The animals in the mixture are not to be offered even by treating them strictly as the stricter kind of sacrifice (for example, slaughtering both in the north like most holy offerings).

for we do not bring consecrated animals to a state of disqualification. We do not bring consecrated animals into a situation in which they will be disqualified or which will cause them to be disqualified (as below, halakhah 6). And if one offers the burnt offering and the peace offering, he will bring their flesh to disqualification, for he cannot eat it (since there is burnt offering flesh here), and cannot burn it (since there is peace offering flesh here).

and just as we do not reduce their eating time etc.. In order not to bring about a situation in which the flesh of consecrated animals could become disqualified, we do not reduce the possibilities for eating it by shortening the eating time, the people who eat, or the place of eating.
in their eating time. For example, in a mixture of an offering eaten for a day and a night (such as a thanksgiving offering) with an offering eaten for two days (such as a peace offering).
we do not reduce their eaters. For example, in a mixture of an offering eaten by priests only (such as a firstborn) with an offering eaten by anyone (such as a tithe).
nor their place of eating. For example, in a mixture of an offering eaten only in the courtyard (such as a sin offering) with an offering eaten throughout the city (such as a peace offering).
and each one of them shall be sold by itself. So that he will know the price of the best of them and will buy at this price from each kind.

even though he already offered a burnt offering that he was obligated in or peace offerings that he was obligated to offer. For example, during the time until they developed a blemish, the owner brought the offering he was obligated in.

he offers with the price of the mixture another burnt offering and other peace offerings. Although he fulfilled his vow obligation with the offering he already brought, he must still offer a burnt offering with the proceeds of the first offering that was consecrated as a burnt offering, or peace offerings with the proceeds of the offering that was consecrated as peace offerings.

and if he went ahead and offered another sin offering for the sin for which he had separated it, all of them shall die. For the sin offering in the mixture is considered a lost sin offering, and when its owners were atoned for with another, its law is to die (Lechem Mishneh). And since it became mixed with peace offerings, all of them die (as above, halakhah 1).

he buys two animals and redeems etc.. He says that the money of the sin offering, wherever it is, shall be unconsecrated, and one of the animals shall be a sin offering in its place. And he says likewise about the money of the guilt offering for the other animal.
and if his sin offering was already offered. If he offered before he redeemed the money for another animal for his sin offering.

he shall take all the money to the Dead Sea. The money of the sin offering is considered the money of a sin offering that dies (as explained in the previous halakhah), and its law is to go to the Dead Sea (above, 5:1). And since it is mixed together with the money of the guilt offering, all of it goes to the Dead Sea.

his guilt offering was already offered, all falls to the freewill offerings. After he was atoned for with another, the mixed guilt offering money is considered the leftover of a guilt offering, and its law is to fall to the freewill offerings (above, 5:9).

a thanksgiving offering that became mixed with its substitute, both shall be offered and the bread shall be waved with them. When he offers the thanksgiving offering brought as a vow and its substitute, he brings bread only with the first animal he offers (see below, 12:8), and when he offers them together he waves the bread with both.

even though his thanksgiving offering was offered. Although he already brought another animal and fulfilled the obligation of the thanksgiving offering that he was obligated in, he must bring another animal with the price of the thanksgiving offering that became mixed and offer it as a thanksgiving offering.
with the ram of a nazirite. A peace offering that the nazirite brings when he completes his nazirite period, and he brings loaves with it that are waved with the offering.

both of them shall be offered and the bread shall be waved with them. The laws of their service and eating are equal, and therefore he may offer each one for the sake of whomever he wishes, since he does not reduce the eating. And he waves with both of them both the thanksgiving loaves and the nazirite loaves.

both of them shall graze until they have a blemish. And he brings with the price of the better of them an animal and redeems the Passover offering on it. And this animal is offered as a Passover offering if he has not yet offered a Passover offering, or as a peace offering if he has already offered a Passover offering (Hilchot Korban Pesach 4:8).

and they shall be eaten like a firstborn. After the Passover offering is redeemed, both animals are treated as a blemished firstborn, which may not be slaughtered and sold in the market, and whose flesh may not be weighed on a scale in the way ordinary meat is weighed (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 1:12).
a tithe. The animal tithe.
when they have a blemish. And he brings a Passover offering with the price of the better of them (as explained in the previous halakhah).
they shall be eaten like the tithe. Like a blemished tithe animal, whose laws of eating are similar to the laws of eating a blemished firstborn.

a firstborn and a tithe that became mixed shall be eaten with their blemish. Without redemption, but they are not to be offered because they are not equal in their eating (a firstborn is eaten by priests and a tithe by anyone).
they shall graze until they have a blemish. And they will buy with the price of the better animal another animal that will be offered in place of the sacrifice that was mixed.

they shall not be offered. So as not to reduce the eating of the peace offering. For the flesh of a guilt offering is eaten by priests for a day and a night, and the flesh of a peace offering is eaten by anyone for two days and a night.

and if he went ahead and offered his guilt offering, both shall fall to the freewill offerings. When he went ahead and offered another animal as a guilt offering, the guilt offering in the mixture is considered a guilt offering whose owner was atoned for, whose law is that its proceeds fall to the freewill offerings (above, 4:14). And since they are mixed together with the price of the peace offering, all fall to the freewill offerings.

except for a sin offering with a guilt offering etc.. For a guilt offering comes from a lamb or a ram, and a sin offering comes from a ewe or a female goat (individual sin offerings) or from a male goat (communal sin offerings and the sin offering of a prince).
and all of these that are mixed while alive. And are forbidden to be offered when they are mixed.
for living creatures are not rejected. And they were not disqualified by being forbidden to be offered in the first instance (see also above, halakhah 1).
from Jerusalem to Migdal Eder. A place near Jerusalem.

and its measure in every direction. This distance from Jerusalem in all directions. And since most of the animals in Jerusalem were sacrifices, we assume that an animal found in Jerusalem and its surroundings is a consecrated animal that ran away from its owner.
he gathers it into a pen. He brings it into an enclosed place.
lest it be a sin offering. And we are concerned that this animal may be one of the sin offerings that must die.

if it was two years old, he shall bring it as peace offerings. For the other sacrifices (burnt offering, guilt offering, firstborn, tithe, and Passover offering) do not come from females, and a sin offering is valid only in its first year, so this animal is certainly a peace offering animal.

there is no remedy for it, lest it be a guilt offering and its owners have not yet been atoned for. If this animal is a guilt offering and its owners were not atoned for, even if it grazes and develops a blemish they will have to bring another guilt offering with its proceeds. And it is impossible to offer it, or what was brought with its proceeds, as a guilt offering out of doubt, since it is not known whether it is really a guilt offering and whether its owners were atoned for or not.
he found a male in its first year. And there is doubt whether it is a burnt offering or a peace offering.
and he brings two animals in its place. Two animals as good as the animal that was found.

and he offers one as a burnt offering, and its libations are from the community's funds. The fine flour and wine that must be brought with the sacrifice are brought from public funds (see also Hilchot Shekalim 4:3), and the court enacted this lest they leave the animal and run away without offering it (Mishnah, Shekalim 7:5; but he brings the libations of the peace offering from his own, since he gains the flesh of the peace offering and there is no concern that he will run away - Or Sameach).
and what shall he do with this one that was found. After it developed a blemish.
it shall be eaten with its blemish. Like a firstborn and a tithe that developed a blemish.

and if it is a Passover offering past its time, it is a peace offering. Bringing a peace offering with its price also covers the possibility that this animal was consecrated as a Passover offering and Passover passed and they did not offer it, for a Passover offering whose time has passed is offered as a peace offering.
and in its season everyone is careful with it. Before Passover everyone is careful not to lose the Passover offering.
lest it be a guilt offering of a nazirite or a leper. Which are brought as males in their first year.
consecrated animals were mixed with consecrated animals after they were slaughtered. Pieces of flesh of sacrifices that became mixed together.
they shall be eaten like the stricter of them. The flesh shall be eaten in the place, at the time, and by the people fit for eating the flesh of both sacrifices.
among disqualified consecrated animals. The flesh of sacrifices that were disqualified and whose law is to be burned.
among unconsecrated animals slaughtered in the courtyard. And they are forbidden for benefit.
their form shall pass. He shall wait until they spoil and are no longer fit for eating.

limbs of a sin offering that became mixed with limbs of a burnt offering. It is impossible to burn the flesh in the mixture because the limbs of the sin offering must be eaten, and it is impossible to eat the flesh because the limbs of the burnt offering must be burned.
and they burn them in the courtyard in the place where they burn disqualified consecrated animals. See Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 7:3.
limbs of blemished animals. Which it is forbidden to burn.
that became mixed with limbs of consecrated animals. Which must be burned on the altar.
and even if all were offered except one of the mixture, it shall be burned. Perhaps this limb is that of the blemished animal.
it shall be removed. The impure piece is nullified in a hundred, and it is permitted to eat the entire mixture as pure consecrated food.
as we have explained in the laws of terumah. That impure terumah is nullified in a hundred and the entire mixture may be eaten as pure terumah (Hilchot Terumot 14:14).

these shall not be removed, but all shall be eaten by the priests. In this case, since the priests are permitted to eat the entire mixture, they must eat it at the time and place permitted for eating the flesh of the sin offering and the showbread, and the consecrated items are not nullified in unconsecrated ones.
like all mixtures of terumah. Unconsecrated produce into which terumah fell, which must be eaten as terumah (ibid. 13:2).
their pinching is invalid. Unlike the slaughter of consecrated animals, which is valid by disqualified people (above, 1:1).

it is not like the carcass of a pure bird with regard to impurity. By Torah law, a person who swallows the carcass of a pure bird becomes impure, and while the carcass is in the throat, it makes the clothes he touches impure (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 3:1). But a bird offering that was pinched in the courtyard, even if the pinching was invalid and the bird was disqualified for the altar, is not considered a carcass.
and likewise if he pinched at night. For its service is invalid.

or he slaughtered unconsecrated animals inside and consecrated animals outside. Although in both of these cases the bird is disqualified from eating, since the bird was slaughtered it does not become a carcass.

turtledoves whose time has not yet come and young pigeons whose time has passed. Turtledoves are valid for an offering only when they are mature, and pigeons only when they are young (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 3:2).
and one whose wing dried up, whose eye was blinded, and whose leg was cut off. Major blemishes that disqualify birds (ibid., halakhah 1).
its wing. Its wing.
it is a carcass for all purposes. Since the bird was not fit for an offering at all, the pinching is not considered an act of slaughter but a killing that makes it a carcass.
anything whose disqualification was in the sanctuary. A bird that was valid for an offering and was disqualified afterward.
therefore one who pinches and it is found to be a treifah. Since a treifah bird is disqualified from offering, the pinching makes it a carcass.
who pinched with a knife. He cut the signs of slaughter from the nape, and this action is not considered pinching at all and makes the bird a carcass.
who pinched unconsecrated animals inside. Since it is not fit for an offering, the pinching makes it a carcass.
and consecrated animals outside. Bird offerings that were pinched outside the courtyard are invalid. And since this disqualification occurred outside, the pinching makes them carcasses.
pinching permits. To offer on the altar.
and purifies. It considers the bird as slaughtered with regard to the impurity of the carcass of a pure bird.
something that is valid for the altar. A bird offering that was pinched in the courtyard.
but one who was bestially copulated with, etc.. In these cases it is simple that their law is that of a carcass for all purposes (Radbaz).
one who was bestially copulated with. That was copulated with by a person.
and one set aside and one worshiped. For idolatry.
and the harlot's fee. Given as payment for a forbidden relationship.
and the dog's price. Given as payment in the sale of a dog.
these are carcasses for all purposes. Since they are not fit for an offering.
and they make clothes impure in the throat. It makes impure the clothes that one touches while the carcass is in his throat.

for sanctity does not take hold of them. For when one consecrates a tumtum or androgynos, sanctity does not take hold of their bodies, and even the other disqualified animals mentioned here have the law of animals with a permanent blemish that are not fit for the altar (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 3:10).

we have already explained in the laws of the performance of the offerings that the bird sin offering is done below. The sprinkling of its blood on the lower part of the altar (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 7:6), and its pinching is valid anywhere on the altar (ibid., halakhah 9).
and the bird burnt offering above. Its pinching (at the surrounding ledge) and the draining of its blood on the upper part of the altar (ibid. 6:20).
a bird sin offering that he did above is invalid. He sprinkled its blood on the upper part of the altar.
whether he made its sprinkling like the act of a sin offering. Sprinkling.
or whether he made it like the act of a burnt offering. Draining.
a bird burnt offering that he did below. He pinched on the lower part of the altar.
one sign. One of the signs of slaughter, the windpipe or the gullet.
whether he pinched it like the pinching of a burnt offering. Severing the head from the body.
or whether he did it like the act of a sin offering. Cutting the signs and leaving the head attached to the body.
a bird sin offering that he pinched below. In its proper place.
like the act of a sin offering for the sake of a burnt offering... invalid. Like a sin offering that was slaughtered not for its own sake (below, 15:1).
a bird burnt offering that he did above. In its proper place.

like the act of a burnt offering for the sake of a sin offering, valid, provided etc.. The offering is valid but the owners did not fulfill their obligation with it and must bring another offering, like any burnt offering that was slaughtered not for its own sake (below, 15:1).
that comes for a doubt. When it is in doubt whether he is liable.
and it is not eaten. Lest he is not liable and it is unconsecrated (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:7).
but it shall be burned like all disqualified consecrated animals. In the courtyard.

a doubtful zavah or a doubtful woman who gave birth. Zavot and women who gave birth bring a bird sin offering (and burnt offering) when they complete their purification, and when they do not know with certainty whether they became impure with the impurity of zivah or childbirth they bring a sin offering out of doubt.
and anything similar to it. The other people lacking atonement (a zav and a leper) who are in doubt whether they are obligated in an offering.
as will be explained in the laws of unintentional sins. 8:1.
